<reason>Side B won by identifying a fatal dilemma for the proposition: if "as strict as traditional media" merely means requiring clear, conspicuous disclosure (as Side A conceded in A2.6 and A4.4), then binding consumer-protection rules already mandate this for influencers (B1.1, B2.1), making the motion redundant. If it means importing broadcast-level compliance machinery—pre-screening unscripted content, logging every furnished prop—then it is unworkable for digital creators and creates disclosure fatigue that obscures real ads (B2.3, B4.6). Side A opened with strong moral framing about equal influence, but repeatedly mischaracterized Side B as defending "voluntary guidelines" despite B's explicit citations of binding laws, and struggled to explain what additional strictness beyond current rules the motion actually requires. Side B maintained a consistent structural distinction between scripted broadcast media and unscripted influencer content, and effectively exposed Side A's retreat from the extreme microphone example (A2.3) in the pressure question round.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.1-B4.6), which exposed the redundancy dilemma: demonstrating that Side A's motion either codifies disclosure standards that already exist (making the proposition vacuous) or imposes unworkable broadcast-style pre-screening on unscripted livestreams (creating disclosure fatigue), while also correcting Side A's strawman characterization of current regulations as "voluntary."</best_rebuttal>
